+# GitHub Actions Self-Hosted Runner on Cube Sandbox
+
+This guide shows how to run ephemeral GitHub Actions self-hosted runners in Cube Sandbox by using [`jimyag/e2b-github-runner`](https://github.com/jimyag/e2b-github-runner). The runner service listens for GitHub `workflow_job` webhook events, creates a Cube sandbox through the E2B-compatible API, registers an ephemeral runner inside that sandbox, and removes the sandbox when the job exits.
+
+## Integration Target and Version
+
+- Integration target: GitHub Actions self-hosted runner
+- Adapter service: [`jimyag/e2b-github-runner`](https://github.com/jimyag/e2b-github-runner)
+- Cube requirement: a reachable CubeAPI endpoint, default `http://<cube-host>:3000`
+- Runner mode: repository-level or organization-level self-hosted runner
+
+```mermaid
+flowchart LR
+  A[GitHub workflow job queued] --> B[GitHub webhook]
+  B --> C[e2b-github-runner]
+  C --> D[CubeAPI E2B-compatible API]
+  D --> E[Cube Sandbox]
+  E --> F[Ephemeral GitHub runner]
+  F --> G[GitHub Actions job]
+```
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- A running Cube Sandbox deployment. See [Quick Start](../quickstart.md), [PVM Deployment](../pvm-deploy.md), or [Bare-Metal Deployment](../bare-metal-deploy.md).
+- A Cube template that can run the GitHub Actions runner process. The template image should include basic build tools needed by your workflows, such as `bash`, `curl`, `tar`, `git`, and any language runtimes used by your jobs.
+- Network access from `e2b-github-runner` to CubeAPI, and data-plane access to CubeProxy. For production, configure wildcard DNS and TLS as described in [HTTPS & Domain Resolution](../https-and-domain.md).
+- A public HTTPS endpoint that GitHub can call for webhook delivery.
+- A GitHub token with permission to create self-hosted runner registration tokens.
+
+Before wiring the GitHub App or webhook, verify the Cube control plane and data plane separately:
+
+```bash
+# CubeAPI control plane
+curl -fsS http://<cube-host>:3000/health
+
+# CubeProxy HTTPS data plane port on the client host that runs e2b-github-runner
+nc -vz <cube-proxy-host> 443
+
+# Wildcard sandbox DNS must resolve to the CubeProxy host.
+getent hosts 49983-test.cube.app

review_comments.body:
**Overly broad token permission**

`Administration: Read and write` is the most permissive repository permission available — it grants the ability to modify repository settings, branch protection rules, rename/delete the repo, etc. The GitHub API call to create a runner registration token does not require this broad a scope.

Consider recommending `Administration: Read` or, if the adapter only needs to create registration tokens, investigating whether a more narrowly scoped permission suffices. For organization-level runners, a GitHub App with `Organization self-hosted runners: Read and write` is more scoped than a PAT with admin org permissions.

+# GitHub Actions Self-Hosted Runner on Cube Sandbox
+
+This guide shows how to run ephemeral GitHub Actions self-hosted runners in Cube Sandbox by using [`jimyag/e2b-github-runner`](https://github.com/jimyag/e2b-github-runner). The runner service listens for GitHub `workflow_job` webhook events, creates a Cube sandbox through the E2B-compatible API, registers an ephemeral runner inside that sandbox, and removes the sandbox when the job exits.
+
+## Integration Target and Version
+
+- Integration target: GitHub Actions self-hosted runner
+- Adapter service: [`jimyag/e2b-github-runner`](https://github.com/jimyag/e2b-github-runner)
+- Cube requirement: a reachable CubeAPI endpoint, default `http://<cube-host>:3000`
+- Runner mode: repository-level or organization-level self-hosted runner
+
+```mermaid
+flowchart LR
+  A[GitHub workflow job queued] --> B[GitHub webhook]
+  B --> C[e2b-github-runner]
+  C --> D[CubeAPI E2B-compatible API]
+  D --> E[Cube Sandbox]
+  E --> F[Ephemeral GitHub runner]
+  F --> G[GitHub Actions job]
+```
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- A running Cube Sandbox deployment. See [Quick Start](../quickstart.md), [PVM Deployment](../pvm-deploy.md), or [Bare-Metal Deployment](../bare-metal-deploy.md).
+- A Cube template that can run the GitHub Actions runner process. The template image should include basic build tools needed by your workflows, such as `bash`, `curl`, `tar`, `git`, and any language runtimes used by your jobs.
+- Network access from `e2b-github-runner` to CubeAPI, and data-plane access to CubeProxy. For production, configure wildcard DNS and TLS as described in [HTTPS & Domain Resolution](../https-and-domain.md).
+- A public HTTPS endpoint that GitHub can call for webhook delivery.
+- A GitHub token with permission to create self-hosted runner registration tokens.
+
+## GitHub Token Permissions
+
+For repository runners, use a fine-grained personal access token when possible:
+
+- Repository access: select only the target repository.
+- Repository permissions: set `Administration` to `Read and write`.
+
+For organization runners, the token must be allowed to manage organization self-hosted runners. The service uses GitHub's runner registration token APIs for the configured scope.
+
+## Configure the Runner Service
+
+Clone and configure the adapter service:
+
+```bash
+git clone https://github.com/jimyag/e2b-github-runner.git
+cd e2b-github-runner
+```
+
+Required environment variables:
+
+```bash
+export E2B_API_URL="http://<cube-host>:3000"
+export E2B_API_KEY="<cube-api-key-or-dummy>"
+export E2B_DOMAIN="<cube-sandbox-domain>"
+export SANDBOX_TEMPLATE_ID="<cube-template-id>"
+
+export GITHUB_TOKEN="<github-token>"
+export GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET="<random-webhook-secret>"
+```
+
+Use repository scope:
+
+```bash
+export RUNNER_SCOPE="repo"
+export GITHUB_OWNER="<repo-owner>"
+export GITHUB_REPO="<repo-name>"
+```
+
+Or use organization scope:
+
+```bash
+export RUNNER_SCOPE="org"
+export GITHUB_ORG="<org-name>"
+```
+
+Common optional settings:
+
+```bash
+export HTTP_ADDR=":8080"
+export STATE_DIR="./var/runners"
+export RUNNER_LABELS="self-hosted,e2b"
+export SANDBOX_TIMEOUT_SECONDS="3600"
+export MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNNERS="1"
+```
+
+Notes:
+
+- `E2B_API_URL` points to CubeAPI, not CubeProxy.
+- `E2B_API_KEY` can be any non-empty value for a local unauthenticated Cube deployment. If Cube authentication is enabled, use a real key accepted by your auth callback.
+- `E2B_DOMAIN` must match the sandbox domain published by CubeAPI. The default quick-start domain is usually `cube.app`; production deployments should use a domain with wildcard DNS.
+- `RUNNER_LABELS` must match the labels used by your GitHub Actions workflow.
+
+## Start the Runner Service
+
+Run the service locally:
+
+```bash
+go run ./cmd/runnerd
+```
+
+Check the health endpoint:
+
+```bash
+curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
+```
+
+For production, run the service under a process manager or package it as a container. Keep `STATE_DIR` on persistent storage so control-plane logs survive service restarts.
+
+## Expose the GitHub Webhook Endpoint
+
+GitHub must be able to reach the service at:
+
+```text
+POST https://<public-host>/webhooks/github
+```
+
+For local testing, expose port `8080` with a tunnel:
+
+```bash
+ngrok http 8080
+```
+
+or:
+
+```bash
+cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8080
+```
+
+For production, put the service behind your ingress or reverse proxy and terminate HTTPS there.
+
+## Configure the GitHub Webhook
+
+In the target repository or organization, add a webhook:
+
+- Payload URL: `https://<public-host>/webhooks/github`
+- Content type: `application/json`
+- Secret: the exact value of `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`
+- Events: select `Workflow jobs`
+- Active: enabled
+
+The service only acts on `workflow_job` events. Other event types can be ignored.
+
+## Use the Runner in a Workflow
+
+Add a workflow that targets the configured labels:
+
+```yaml
+name: cube-runner-smoke
+
+on:
+  workflow_dispatch:
+
+jobs:
+  smoke:
+    runs-on: [self-hosted, e2b]
+    steps:
+      - name: Print runner info
+        run: |
+          uname -a
+          whoami
+          pwd
+```
+
+Expected flow:
+
+1. GitHub queues a job with labels `self-hosted` and `e2b`.
+2. GitHub sends a `workflow_job.queued` webhook.
+3. `e2b-github-runner` validates the webhook signature and creates a Cube sandbox.
+4. The service requests a GitHub runner registration token and starts an ephemeral runner inside the sandbox.
+5. GitHub assigns the job to the sandbox runner.
+6. When the runner exits, the service cleans up the sandbox.
+
+## Troubleshooting
+
+Check active runner requests:
+
+```bash
+curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/runners | jq
+```
+
+Inspect per-request state and logs:
+
+```bash
+cat var/runners/<request_id>/state.json

review_comments.body:
**Suggestion: Add webhook secret generation guidance**

Replace the placeholder with a concrete generation command so users don't pick a weak secret:

```bash
# Generate a strong random webhook secret
GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET=$(python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))")
```

A weak webhook secret allows an attacker to forge GitHub webhook events, triggering unauthorized sandbox provisioning.

review_comments.body:
**Security: Use HTTPS for the control-plane channel**

Plain HTTP transmits the `E2B_API_KEY` credential and all sandbox management commands in cleartext over the network. If the runner service and CubeAPI are not on the same host (common in production), this enables credential eavesdropping.

Recommendation: Use `https://` by default and add a note recommending HTTPS for production deployments:

```
export E2B_API_URL="https://<cube-host>:3000"
```

Then in the Notes section (line 97), add: "Use HTTPS for `E2B_API_URL` in production to protect the API key and sandbox management commands from network eavesdropping."

## Code Review

### Summary

This PR adds a blank import for the metric plugin (`Cubelet/plugins/cube/internals/metric`) in `builtins.go`. Without this import, the plugin's `init()` function never executes, and containerd's plugin system never registers the metric service, causing the `/v1/metrics/scheduler` endpoint to return 404.

### What was checked

- **Diff correctness**: The added import is in alphabetical order within the `cube/internals/*` import block — it's correctly placed between `cubes` and `netfile`.
- **Plugin registration**: The metric plugin (`plugin.go` line 44) uses `registry.Register()` in its `init()`, so a blank import is the correct and sufficient mechanism to trigger registration.
- **Pattern consistency**: This follows the same convention as all other plugins in the file (e.g., `sandbox`, `cgroup`, `createid`, `images`, etc.).

### Finding

**LGTM — the change is correct and minimal.** The single-line addition is exactly what's needed. No issues found.

### Minor note (pre-existing, not related to this PR)

There's a duplicate import of `cube/multimeta` at lines 69 and 74. This is unrelated to the fix here, but worth cleaning up in a follow-up since duplicate imports are a dead code smell.

## PR Review: feat(web): add WebUI with sandbox/template/node management and template store

### Overview
This is a large PR (6161 additions, 348 deletions across 71 files) that adds significant WebUI functionality along with backend API support. The main areas are:

- **New pages**: Network, Observability, Settings, TemplateStore, SandboxNew, NodeDetail, enhanced TemplateDetail
- **New backend endpoints**: `/config`, `/store/meta`, `/store/refresh`, sandbox logs streaming (CubeMaster)
- **i18n**: Full zh/en localization for all new pages
- **Data-layer enhancements**: Template network fields, node quota fields, sandbox creation via API

---

### 🐛 Bug: `qc` is undefined in `TemplateStorePage` 

**File**: `web/src/pages/TemplateStore.tsx:453-480`

The `checkUpdates` mutation references `qc` (QueryClient), but `qc` is **not declared** in the `TemplateStorePage` component scope — it's only declared inside the nested `InstallModal` component. This will cause a **runtime ReferenceError** when the "Check Updates" button is clicked.

```tsx
const { mutate: checkUpdates, isPending: isChecking } = useMutation({
  mutationFn: storeApi.refresh,
  onSuccess: (data) => {
    qc.setQueryData(['store-meta'], data);  // ❌ qc is not defined
  },
});
```

Fix: Add `const qc = useQueryClient();` at the top of `TemplateStorePage`.

---

### ⚠️ Issues

**1. Hardcoded Chinese toast in global hotkey handler**

**File**: `web/src/hooks/useGlobalHotkeys.ts:49`

The `R` key shortcut dispatches a hardcoded Chinese toast message "已刷新". This should use i18n since the app supports zh/en switching.

```tsx
window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('cube:toast', { detail: { message: '已刷新' } }));
```

[Fix this →](https://claude.ai/code?q=In+web/src/hooks/useGlobalHotkeys.ts%2C+replace+the+hardcoded+Chinese+toast+message+%27%E5%B7%B2%E5%88%B7%E6%96%B0%27+with+an+i18n+key+using+the+observability+namespace%2C+at+line+49+of+the+current+branch+feat%2Fwebui-clean)

**2. Hardcoded Chinese section headers in TemplateDetail**

**File**: `web/src/pages/TemplateDetail.tsx:462-463,475-476`

The "规格" (Specs) and "属性" (Attributes) sub-section headers are hardcoded in Chinese, while the rest of the page uses i18n. These should be added to the `templateDetail.json` locale files.

**3. Aggressive polling in TemplateStore**

**File**: `web/src/pages/TemplateStore.tsx:443`

```tsx
refetchInterval: 5000,  // 5s polling
```

Polling all templates every 5 seconds is intensive. Consider increasing to 15-30s unless real-time updates are essential for the install flow. The install modal already has its own 2s polling mechanism.

**4. Duplicate `/config` queries across components**

The `/config` endpoint is independently queried in:
- `Settings.tsx` (ClusterSection + AboutSection — same query key, should share)
- `Observability.tsx` (ApiSection)
- `Network.tsx` (GatewaySection)

Each has a different `staleTime` (30s, 60s, 60s). While React Query deduplicates in-flight requests, having slightly different cache policies can lead to unexpected refetches. Consider standardizing the stale time or extracting a shared hook.

**5. Docker subprocess in API server**

**File**: `CubeAPI/src/handlers/store.rs:65-68,149-153`

The `GET /store/meta` and `POST /store/refresh` handlers execute `docker image inspect` and `docker pull` subprocesses from the API server. While currently safe (image names are hardcoded in `STORE_IMAGES`), this pattern:

- Creates a dependency on the Docker CLI being available in the CubeAPI runtime
- The `refresh` endpoint triggers unbounded network pulls that can take minutes
- Consider having a background task handle pulls instead of blocking the HTTP response

---

### ✅ What's done well

- **Consistent UI patterns**: Skeleton loading states, error handling, empty states — nearly every component handles all three states
- **Clean component decomposition**: Each page is broken into focused sub-components (e.g., `InstallModal`, `InstalledDropdown`, `StoreCard` in TemplateStore)
- **i18n coverage**: All new pages have complete zh/en locale files
- **Backward-compatible API changes**: New fields use `Option<T>` / `#[serde(default)]` so existing clients are unaffected
- **Thoughtful resource calculations**: The cluster service's sandbox-aggregated resource usage calculation (`fetch_used_resources`) is a nice improvement over raw CubeMaster allocatable values
- **Error boundary awareness**: The TemplateDetail page handles 404s, building-in-progress, and build-failed states gracefully

---

### Summary

| Category | Count |
|----------|-------|
| 🐛 Bugs | 1 (critical: undefined `qc` in TemplateStorePage) |
| ⚠️ Issues | 5 (i18n, performance, architecture) |
| ✅ Good practices | 6 |

The most pressing issue is the **undefined `qc` variable** in `TemplateStore.tsx` — clicking "Check Updates" will throw a runtime error. The remaining items are quality improvements that can be addressed iteratively.

### Code Review: `feat(template): support --user flag and respect image User field`

**Change Summary**

Two files modified:
- `CubeMaster/cmd/cubemastercli/commands/cubebox/template.go` — Added `--user` CLI flag and `parseContainerOverrides` handles it
- `CubeMaster/pkg/templatecenter/template_image.go` — Added `User` field to `dockerImageConfig`, `applyUserToSecurityContext()` helper, and wired image User into `generateTemplateCreateRequest` with proper override semantics

---

**Overall Impression**

The PR is well-structured and follows the existing override pattern (env/cmd/workingdir). The fix addresses a real bug where `imageCfg.User` was parsed from Docker inspect but never applied. Good separation of concerns with the `applyUserToSecurityContext` helper.

---

### Issues & Suggestions

#### 1. `groupPart` silently ignored for non-numeric group in `applyUserToSecurityContext` (template_image.go:112-116)

```go
if groupPart != "" {
    if gid, err := strconv.ParseInt(groupPart, 10, 64); err == nil {
        securityContext.RunAsGroup = &types.Int64Value{Value: gid}
    }
}
```

If a user specifies `--user node:groupname`, the group portion is silently dropped because `ParseInt` fails and there's no `RunAsGroupName` field fallback. Consider logging a warning or returning an error. The same issue exists in the CLI-side parsing at `template.go:1446-1449`.

#### 2. `Privileged: true` always set for image-derived User (template_image.go:1613)

```go
securityContext := &types.ContainerSecurityContext{Privileged: true, ReadonlyRootfs: false}
```

This is then overridden by `ContainerOverrides.SecurityContext`. However, the `Privileged: true` default means all containers from `create-from-image` run privileged. Is this intentional? If so, it's worth a brief comment explaining why (e.g., "rootfs mount requires privileged").

#### 3. Override logic for `RunAsUsername` — potential zero-value conflict (template_image.go:1628)

```go
if override.RunAsUsername != "" {
    securityContext.RunAsUsername = override.RunAsUsername
}
```

If the image User is `1000` (numeric, sets `RunAsUser`) and the user passes `--user ""` (empty string), the override won't trigger because `"" == ""`. However, this matches the pattern used for other fields like `WorkingDir`, so it's consistent — just worth noting that there's no way to "unset" a user back to empty via the CLI.

#### 4. Both `RunAsUser` and `RunAsUsername` could be set simultaneously

If a Docker image has `USER 1000` and the user passes `--user node`, the resulting `SecurityContext` will have both `RunAsUser = 1000` and `RunAsUsername = "node"`. This could be confusing — Kubernetes allows it, but the behavior depends on the runtime. Consider clearing the other field when setting one:

```go
if override.RunAsUser != nil {
    securityContext.RunAsUser = override.RunAsUser
    securityContext.RunAsUsername = "" // clear username if setting UID
}
if override.RunAsUsername != "" {
    securityContext.RunAsUsername = override.RunAsUsername
    securityContext.RunAsUser = nil // clear UID if setting username
}
```

#### 5. `parseContainerOverrides` — `userFlag` check uses `c.String()` instead of `c.IsSet()` (template.go:1378)

```go
if len(cmds) == 0 && len(args) == 0 && len(rawEnvs) == 0 && len(dnsServers) == 0 && probePort == 0 && !c.IsSet("cpu") && !c.IsSet("memory") && userFlag == "" {
```

This early return skips building a `ContainerOverrides` entirely. Since `userFlag == ""` when `--user` is not set, this correctly falls through. However, if someone sets `--user ""` explicitly, it still returns nil. This is minor and unlikely to be a real issue in practice.

#### 6. `SecurityContext.RunAsGroup` field name mismatch (template_image.go:112-116)

The `applyUserToSecurityContext` function uses the field name `RunAsGroup`, but the override block at line 1625-1627 also uses `RunAsGroup`. This is consistent within the PR — just confirming that `Int64Value` is the correct type (consistent with `RunAsUser`).

---

### Positive Highlights

- ✅ **Consistent override pattern**: `--user` flag overrides image `User`, matching the existing `--cmd`/`--env`/`--workingdir` pattern
- ✅ **Helper extraction**: `applyUserToSecurityContext` is clean and reusable
- ✅ **Docker USER format support**: Handles `user`, `uid`, `user:group`, `uid:gid` formats
- ✅ **CLI flag added with usage**: Clear usage text on the `--user` flag
- ✅ **No breaking changes**: Existing behavior unchanged when `--user` is not specified

---

### Summary

This is a clean, focused fix. The main concern is the potential for both `RunAsUser` and `RunAsUsername` being set simultaneously (item 4), and the silent dropping of non-numeric group names (item 1). Everything else is minor.

---
## Code Review: `feat/webui-dev`

This PR adds substantial WebUI functionality — new pages (Network, Observability, Settings, TemplateStore, TemplateDetail, NodeDetail, SandboxNew), enhanced existing pages, backend handlers (store metadata, config, cluster improvements), sandbox log streaming in Go, i18n resources, and documentation.

**Commit summary**: 53 commits, 70 files, +6223/−341

---

### Notable Issues & Suggestions

#### `web/src/components/ui/ToastProvider.tsx` — Broken JSX attribute syntax

The `className` prop on the container `<div>` at line 50 uses `=fixed` instead of `="fixed ..."` (missing quotes around the class string). This will cause a React build error.

```tsx
// Current (broken) — line 50
<div className=fixed bottom-6 left-1/2 ...>
```
Similarly on lines 63 and 65, `className=h-3.5 w-3.5` is missing quotes.

**Fix**: Add quotes around all `className` values.

#### `web/src/data/templateStore.ts` — `writable_layer_size` field unused across all definitions

The `writable_layer_size` field is defined as `'1G'` in all three template entries. Meanwhile, in `StoreTemplate`'s `writable_layer_size` property, it's `'1G'` for all entries. This is minor but could be simplified if it's always the same value.

#### `web/src/pages/TemplateStore.tsx` — Hardcoded Chinese text

The TemplateStore page (`TemplateStore.tsx`) and its `InstallModal` component use hardcoded Chinese user-facing strings (lines 135, 158, 182, 194, 205, 210, 218, 226, 228, 229, 289, 313, 377, 383, 420, 495, 497, 512, 558) while other pages consistently use `useTranslation` with namespaced locale files. For consistency, these should be moved to i18n locale files (e.g., `templateStore.json`).

#### `web/src/pages/TemplateStore.tsx` — `InstalledDropdown` positional dropdown

The `InstalledDropdown` uses `getBoundingClientRect()` + absolute positioning + `createPortal`. This approach works but is fragile compared to using a library dropdown or a CSS-based positioning strategy. If the page scrolls or the trigger button moves, the dropdown may appear at the wrong coordinates.

#### `web/src/pages/SandboxDetail.tsx` — `formatDateTime` function doesn't use `useTranslation`

The local helper `formatDateTime` at line 243 uses `Intl.DateTimeFormat(undefined, ...)` which falls back to the browser's default locale rather than the user's selected i18n language. Other pages use `useTranslation` + `formatRelative` consistently.

#### `web/src/pages/Sandboxes.tsx` — Busy state is shared across all action buttons

The `busy` prop on individual `Row` components at line 148 combines `killMut.isPending || pauseMut.isPending || resumeMut.isPending`. This means while one sandbox is being paused, **all** action buttons on **all** sandbox rows are disabled. This is a poor UX pattern — mutations should be tracked per-sandbox-ID.

#### `CubeAPI/src/handlers/store.rs` — `docker pull` in `refresh_store_meta` is blocking and sequential

The `refresh_store_meta` handler at line 143 pulls images sequentially. With 3 store images (and potentially more in the future), this adds latency. Each `docker pull` could take minutes for large images (e.g., the browser sandbox is ~1.5 GB). Consider parallel pulls with `tokio::join!` or background task dispatch + polling endpoint.

Also, running `docker pull` from an HTTP handler thread is a security concern — it exposes Docker daemon access to anyone who can hit this endpoint. The endpoint should at minimum require authentication.

#### `CubeAPI/src/handlers/store.rs` — `get_store_meta` calls `docker image inspect` which may fail silently

If Docker is not installed or the daemon is not running, `inspect_image` returns `None` and the image is simply omitted from the response without any error or warning. Consider logging on failure.

#### `web/src/pages/NodeDetail.tsx` — `allSandboxes` query fetches all sandboxes

The page fetches all sandboxes via `sandboxApi.list()` at line 129, then filters to only those matching this node. On larger clusters, this could fetch thousands of sandboxes just to display a handful. A server-side filter would be more efficient.

#### `CubeAPI/src/services/templates.rs` — `get_template_build_logs` returns only a single line

The `get_template_build_logs` method at line 245 constructs a JSON response with a single log line. This seems like a placeholder — actual build logs should stream multiple lines.

#### Backend: `CubeMaster/pkg/service/httpservice/cube/sandbox_logs.go` — `readShimLogs` scans the entire file

At line 152, `readShimLogs` iterates through every line in the shim log file with `bufio.Scanner`. For large log files, this becomes increasingly slow. Since the cursor-based pagination skips entries with `tsMs <= cursor`, consider tailing from the end or using a more efficient offset mechanism (e.g., `os.File.Seek` to the approximate position).

#### `web/src/api/client.ts` — Inconsistent error handling for `storeApi`

The `storeApi` at lines 211-214 uses the generic `api()` helper but doesn't map responses like the other APIs (`mapNode`, `mapTemplateSummary`, etc.). This is fine for raw pass-through, but if the API response format differs from what's expected, the error handling will be less graceful.

---

### Overall Assessment

| Area | Rating | Notes |
|------|--------|-------|
| **Frontend architecture** | ✅ Good | Clean React patterns with React Query, proper component composition |
| **UI/UX** | ✅ Good | Consistent design language, loading/empty/error states handled well |
| **i18n** | ⚠️ Partial | Most pages use translation hooks but TemplateStore is hardcoded to Chinese |
| **Backend Rust** | ✅ Good | Well-structured services with proper error mapping |
| **Backend Go** | ✅ Good | Clean addition of sandbox log streaming |
| **Security** | ⚠️ Needs attention | `docker pull` in store handler is unauthenticated |
| **Performance** | ⚠️ Minor concerns | Sequential Docker pulls, full log file scanning, unbatched sandbox mutation state |
| **Tests** | ❌ Missing | Mock fixtures exist for development but no automated tests for new pages |
| **Documentation** | ✅ Good | Thorough design docs and template build practice guide |

### Summary

This is a substantial and well-crafted PR that significantly expands the WebUI's capabilities. The code quality is generally high with clean React patterns, comprehensive state handling, and consistent design. The main areas to address before merging:

1. **Fix the JSX syntax error** in `ToastProvider.tsx` (broken `className` attribute syntax) — this would prevent the app from building
2. **Remove hardcoded Chinese** from `TemplateStore.tsx` in favor of i18n
3. **Secure the store endpoint** — `docker pull` should not be callable without authentication
4. **Consider performance** — sequential image pulls and full log file scanning could be optimized
5. **Add tests** — new pages lack test coverage

## Code Review: Pre-download Preflight Checks

### Overview
This PR adds lightweight pre-download environment checks to `online-install.sh` and reorders checks in `install.sh` to fail fast. Overall, this is a **well-structured and valuable change** that addresses a real user pain point. The code is clean and the documentation updates are thorough. Below are my findings.

---

### ✅ What's Done Well

1. **Clear separation of concerns** — The early preflight checks in `online-install.sh` are self-contained (no external dependencies) and run before any download begins. The reordering in `install.sh` correctly moves the checks before dependency installation.

2. **Thoughtful `--skip-precheck` design** — Supporting both an env var (`ONE_CLICK_SKIP_PRECHECK`) and a CLI flag (`--skip-precheck`) covers both piping patterns (`curl ... | bash` with env var, and `bash -s --` with arguments). Good UX.

3. **Smart directory traversal for XFS check** — Walking up from `/data/cubelet` to find the closest existing parent path handles the common case where `/data/` exists but `/data/cubelet/` doesn't exist yet. The loop termination guard (`[[ "${parent}" != "${check_path}" ]] || break`) prevents infinite loops.

4. **Graceful curl/wget fallback** — The command check correctly requires only one of `curl` or `wget`, not both. The python3 check only applies when `--url` is omitted. These show good attention to edge cases.

5. **Documentation is bilingual and clear** — Both English and Chinese docs are updated with proper examples for both bypass methods. The warning about `install.sh` still enforcing constraints is well-placed.

---

### 🔍 Issues to Address

#### 1. Duplicated memory threshold validation logic
**File:** `deploy/one-click/online-install.sh` (lines ~89-108) and `deploy/one-click/install.sh` (lines ~152-166)

The `CUBE_MIN_MEMORY_KB` parsing + validation + floor enforcement is duplicated verbatim between the two scripts. If the threshold logic ever changes (e.g., new validation rules, different floor value), both files must be updated in lockstep.

**Suggestion:** Consider extracting the memory check into a shared source that both scripts can source. Since `online-install.sh` downloads and extracts `install.sh`, one approach would be to keep the online preflight checks minimal (only detect unrecoverable failures like missing `/dev/kvm` or non-XFS) and defer the memory check entirely to `install.sh`. Alternatively, a small sourced library file could serve both.

#### 2. Silent floor enforcement for `CUBE_MIN_MEMORY_KB`
**File:** `deploy/one-click/online-install.sh` lines 94-96, `deploy/one-click/install.sh` lines 157-159

```bash
if [[ "${CUBE_MIN_MEMORY_KB}" -ge 7500000 ]]; then
    min_mem_kb="${CUBE_MIN_MEMORY_KB}"
fi
```

If a user sets `CUBE_MIN_MEMORY_KB=4000000` (below the 7500000 floor), the value is silently ignored with no warning. This could confuse users who intentionally set a lower threshold and see no error but also no effect.

**Suggestion:** Add an `else` branch with a warning to stderr:
```bash
else
    echo "[install.sh] WARNING: CUBE_MIN_MEMORY_KB=${CUBE_MIN_MEMORY_KB} is below minimum of 7500000 KB, using default." >&2
fi
```

#### 3. Exit codes are undocumented
The function `check_early_preflight` uses three distinct exit codes:
- `exit 1` — Permission/access errors (not root, not writable)
- `exit 2` — Missing dependencies (commands, python3, package manager)
- `exit 3` — Environment incompatibility (wrong OS, no KVM, low memory, wrong FS)

These are not documented anywhere. The calling context (`online-install.sh`) does not distinguish between them — any non-zero exit will terminate the script. While unused today, documenting the convention would help future maintainers.

**Suggestion:** Add a comment near `check_early_preflight` or at the top of the file:
```bash
# Early preflight exit codes:
#   1 — Permission errors
#   2 — Missing dependencies/tools
#   3 — Environment incompatibility
```

#### 4. Redundant default on SKIP_PRECHECK inside the function
**File:** `deploy/one-click/online-install.sh` line 19

```bash
SKIP_PRECHECK="${ONE_CLICK_SKIP_PRECHECK:-0}"
```
Then inside `check_early_preflight()`:
```bash
if [[ "${SKIP_PRECHECK:-0}" == "1" ]]; then
```

The `:-0` default inside the function is redundant since `SKIP_PRECHECK` is already initialized with a default at the top of the script. Minor, but worth cleaning up.

#### 5. DNS check logic complexity
**File:** `deploy/one-click/online-install.sh` lines 149-179

The DNS readiness check has three levels of nesting:
- If `resolvectl` is absent → check NetworkManager
  - If NetworkManager is not loaded → error
  - If NetworkManager is loaded but `dnsmasq` is not installed
    - If no supported package manager → error

This mirrors logic from `install.sh`, but the intertwined conditions in a flat sequence (no helper functions) make it harder to follow. Consider extracting into a `check_dns_preflight()` helper if this grows further.

#### 6. Path traversal edge case in XFS check
**File:** `deploy/one-click/online-install.sh` lines 114-119

```bash
while [[ ! -e "${check_path}" ]]; do
    local parent
    parent="$(dirname "${check_path}")"
    [[ "${parent}" != "${check_path}" ]] || break
    check_path="${parent}"
done
```

If `/data/cubelet` is a **broken symlink** (not just a non-existent path), `-e` returns false and the loop walks upward. But a broken symlink on an ancestor could cause similar issues. Also, if `/data/cubelet` exists as a non-directory (e.g., a regular file), the subsequent `df -T` usage may behave unexpectedly.

#### 7. Missing `shellcheck`-compatible quoting considerations
Many of the error messages use variable interpolation inside double-quoted strings passed to `echo`, e.g.:
```bash
echo "[online-install] ERROR: Invalid CUBE_MIN_MEMORY_KB '${CUBE_MIN_MEMORY_KB}' (must be a positive integer greater than 0)." >&2
```
This is fine for display purposes, but if these strings are ever logged or processed, the variables are user-influenced. Consider using printf with format strings if trustworthy output is needed later.

---

### 🧪 Testing Considerations

- **Unit testing**: These shell scripts don't appear to have a test suite. Given that the checks are self-contained (no side effects like installing packages), they would be amenable to `bats` (Bash Automated Testing System) tests with mocked `/proc/meminfo`, `uname`, and `df` output.
- **Manual testing matrix**: At minimum, the following scenarios should be tested:
  - All checks pass → download proceeds
  - Each individual check fails → appropriate error + exit code
  - `--skip-precheck` → all checks skipped, download proceeds
  - `ONE_CLICK_SKIP_PRECHECK=1` → same as above
  - Piped install with `--skip-precheck`: `curl ... | bash -s -- --skip-precheck`

---

### Summary

| Area | Verdict |
|------|---------|
| Correctness | ✅ Sound logic, proper exit code categories |
| UX | ✅ Helpful error messages with remediation steps |
| Maintainability | ⚠️ Minor duplication between install.sh and online-install.sh |
| Security | ✅ No injection vectors identified |
| Docs | ✅ Bilingual, accurate examples |
| Shell best practices | ✅ Clean bash, consistent style |

The PR is in good shape. The issues noted are mostly **minor enhancements** — the two I'd prioritize are #2 (warning on silently ignored threshold) and #4 (redundant default), as they're trivial fixes that improve clarity.

---

**Background:**
Under weak networks, I waited 10+ minutes to download the large release bundle, only for `install.sh` to fail immediately due to a non-XFS root filesystem. Since it cleans up temporary directories, I had to fix my partition and redownload the entire bundle all over again.

**Solution:**
Added lightweight pre-download preflight checks (OS, root, RAM, KVM, XFS) directly to `online-install.sh` to fail fast before initiating any download. Also reordered `install.sh` checks to fail before system modifications. Supports a bypass option (`--skip-precheck`).

@@ -7,16 +7,190 @@ GITHUB_API_BASE="https://api.github.com/repos/${GITHUB_REPO}"
 CN_MIRROR_LATEST_URL="https://download.cubesandbox.com/release/latest.json"
 MIRROR="${MIRROR:-}"
 
+SKIP_PRECHECK="${ONE_CLICK_SKIP_PRECHECK:-0}"
 DOWNLOAD_URL="${CUBE_SANDBOX_DOWNLOAD_URL:-}"
 INSTALL_ARGS=()
 
 for arg in "$@"; do
   case "${arg}" in
     --url=*) DOWNLOAD_URL="${arg#--url=}" ;;
+    --skip-precheck) SKIP_PRECHECK=1 ;;
     *)       INSTALL_ARGS+=("${arg}") ;;
   esac
 done
 
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# Pre-download preflight checks (lightweight, self-contained)
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+check_early_preflight() {
+  if [[ "${SKIP_PRECHECK:-0}" == "1" ]]; then
+    echo "[online-install] Skipping pre-download preflight checks." >&2
+    return 0
+  fi
+
+  echo "[online-install] Running pre-download preflight checks..." >&2
+
+  # 1. OS check (Must be first to avoid Linux-specific command/path failures on non-Linux OS)
+  if [[ "$(uname)" != "Linux" ]]; then
+    echo "[online-install] ERROR: Cube Sandbox only supports Linux." >&2
+    exit 3
+  fi
+
+  # 2. Root check (install.sh and services require root anyway)
+  if [[ "${EUID}" -ne 0 ]]; then
+    echo "[online-install] ERROR: This script must run as root." >&2
+    echo "[online-install] Please run with sudo or as root user." >&2
+    exit 1
+  fi
+
+  # 3. Essential commands for downloading and extracting
+  local cmd
+  for cmd in tar awk curl wget; do
+    if ! command -v "${cmd}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+      if [[ "${cmd}" == "curl" || "${cmd}" == "wget" ]]; then
+        # We need at least one of curl or wget to download the bundle
+        if ! command -v curl >/dev/null 2>&1 && ! command -v wget >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+          echo "[online-install] ERROR: required command not found: curl or wget" >&2
+          exit 2
+        fi
+      else
+        echo "[online-install] ERROR: required command not found: ${cmd}" >&2
+        exit 2
+      fi
+    fi
+  done
+
+  # 4. python3 check (needed for JSON release discovery if --url is omitted)
+  if [[ -z "${DOWNLOAD_URL}" ]] && ! command -v python3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+    echo "[online-install] ERROR: required command not found: python3 (needed to parse latest release JSON)" >&2
+    echo "[online-install] Please install python3 or specify the download URL manually with --url=<url>" >&2
+    exit 2
+  fi
+
+  # 5. KVM check
+  if [[ ! -e /dev/kvm ]]; then
+    if [[ "${CUBE_PVM_ENABLE:-0}" == "1" ]]; then
+      echo "[online-install] ERROR: PVM mode is enabled (CUBE_PVM_ENABLE=1), but /dev/kvm was not found." >&2
+      echo "[online-install] Please make sure:" >&2
+      echo "[online-install]   1. You have installed the PVM host kernel and rebooted into it (check with: uname -r)." >&2
+      echo "[online-install]   2. The PVM KVM module is loaded on the host: sudo modprobe kvm_pvm" >&2
+      echo "[online-install] Note: Cube Sandbox requires /dev/kvm to function." >&2
+    else
+      echo "[online-install] ERROR: KVM is not supported or not enabled (/dev/kvm not found)." >&2
+      echo "[online-install] If this host cannot expose hardware KVM (e.g., nested virtualization is disabled)," >&2
+      echo "[online-install] you can use the prebuilt PVM kernel to enable KVM on this host first:" >&2
+      echo "[online-install]   1. Download the prebuilt PVM kernel (RPM/DEB) matching your OS from Releases:" >&2
+      echo "[online-install]        https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/releases" >&2
+      echo "[online-install]   2. Install the package, and set up boot parameters using:" >&2
+      echo "[online-install]        curl -sL https://github.com/tencentcloud/CubeSandbox/raw/master/deploy/pvm/grub/host_grub_config.sh | bash" >&2
+      echo "[online-install]   3. Reboot into PVM kernel, then install Cube Sandbox in PVM mode:" >&2
+      echo "[online-install]        curl -sL https://github.com/tencentcloud/CubeSandbox/raw/master/deploy/one-click/online-install.sh | CUBE_PVM_ENABLE=1 bash" >&2

## Review of PR #286: Revert "deps(rust): bump time to 0.3.47 to fix CVE-2026-25727"

### Summary

This PR selectively reverts the `time` crate bump from #267 (`0.3.47` → `0.3.41` in agent, `0.3.47` → `0.3.36` in hypervisor's transitive dep) while preserving all other security fixes from that PR (`vmm-sys-util`, `bytes`, `env_logger`). 3 files changed. 1 commit.

### Root Cause Verified

`time 0.3.47` → `time-core 0.1.8` → `edition = "2024"` → requires Rust ≥ 1.85.0. The CI environment (`cloud-hypervisor:20240507-0`, cargo 1.77.0) and the project's `rust-toolchain.toml = "1.77.2"` cannot parse the manifest. The failure is a hard blocker at the dependency-resolution stage.

**Severity: 🟢 Correctly identified and cleanly scoped.**

### CVE Risk Assessment

| Aspect | Finding |
|---|---|
| CVE | CVE-2026-25727 — stack-exhaustion DoS via Rfc2822 parsing |
| Codebase usage of `time` | `Rfc3339` for outbound timestamp formatting only (`CubeShim/shim/src/log/mod.rs:18,321,407`) |
| Rfc2822 usage | **None found** anywhere in the codebase |
| CVE reachable? | **No** — the vulnerable codepath is never invoked |
| Risk of revert | **Low** — the attack vector is not present |

### Changes Review

#### 1. `agent/Cargo.toml` — Correct

```
-time = "0.3.47"
+time = "0.3.41"
```

Restores the exact version present before #267 (confirmed against parent commit `6d6b3c57`). No other dependencies touched. ✅

#### 2. `agent/Cargo.lock` — Clean

Only the `time` family of packages (`time`, `time-core`, `time-macros`, `num-conv`) and their transitive `serde` dependency are reverted. No orphaned entries or resolution conflicts. ✅

#### 3. `hypervisor/Cargo.lock` — Clean but note the wider diff

The hypervisor lockfile shows additional reverts (`serde 1.0.228→1.0.209`, `serde_derive`, `syn 2.0.87→2.0.77`, `deranged 0.5.8→0.3.11`) that are **passive lockfile resolution changes**, not manifest changes. These occur because:

- `time 0.3.47` introduced `serde_core` as a crate-level re-export, pulling in newer `serde`/`syn` versions
- With `time` reverted to 0.3.36, the resolver falls back to the older crate versions that were already in the tree

These are **inert** — no code changes, no API changes in the final binary. ✅

### Suggestions

None. This is a clean, minimal, well-scoped revert. The PR description accurately documents:

- The root cause (edition2024 + MSRV mismatch)
- Why a re-revert is acceptable (CVE not reachable)
- Why not to bump MSRV instead (downstream `rust-toolchain.toml = "1.77.2"` constraint)
- What was verified (`cargo metadata --locked`, `make shim`)

### Questions

- Are there plans to upgrade the CI Docker image (`cloud-hypervisor:20240507-0`) to a newer Rust version in a follow-up? Re-landing the `time` bump would be possible once CI ships Rust ≥ 1.85.0.
- Could `time` be isolated behind a feature flag on the hypervisor crate to allow the agent crate (which already uses `time` in its manifest) to consume 0.3.47 independently?

## Summary

The `time 0.3.47` portion of #267 broke `hypervisor-integration` CI.
Revert that single bump while keeping the other security fixes from
#267 (vmm-sys-util, bytes, env_logger).

## Why

`time 0.3.47` pins `time-core =0.1.8`, which is the first `time-core`
release that uses `edition = "2024"`. `edition2024` requires Rust
>= 1.85.0, but:

- `hypervisor/Cargo.toml` declares `rust-version = "1.77.0"`
- `hypervisor-integration.yaml` runs `dev_cli.sh tests` against
  `ghcr.io/cloud-hypervisor/cloud-hypervisor:20240507-0`, which ships
  `cargo 1.77.0`

So CI fails at the manifest-parsing stage:

error: failed to parse manifest at .../time-core-0.1.8/Cargo.toml feature edition2024 is required


## Why It's Safe to Revert the Time Bump

CVE-2026-25727 is a stack-exhaustion DoS that requires parsing
**user-controlled input with the RFC 2822 format**. This codebase
only uses `time::format_description::well_known::Rfc3339` (in
`CubeShim/shim/src/log/mod.rs`) for outbound timestamp formatting,
and never invokes Rfc2822 parsing on untrusted input. The vulnerable
attack vector is not reachable here.

## Why Not Just Bump CI / MSRV

Raising the MSRV would conflict with downstream constraints: cube-shim
uses `rust-toolchain.toml = "1.77.2"` and links the hypervisor crate
through a path dependency, so the hypervisor library must remain
buildable on the same toolchain.

## Verification

- `cargo metadata --locked` succeeds in `hypervisor/` under
  `cloud-hypervisor:20240507-0` (cargo 1.77.0).
- `make shim` succeeds end-to-end.
- Diff is minimal: 3 files (`agent/Cargo.toml`, `agent/Cargo.lock`,
  `hypervisor/Cargo.lock`), restoring exactly the pre-#267 state of
  the `time` family.

## Review: LlamaIndex Integration Guide

This is a well-structured documentation PR that adds a bilingual (EN/ZH) LlamaIndex integration guide following the project's contribution guidelines. The code examples are clear and the guide covers the full lifecycle from setup to advanced use cases.

### What's good

- **Bilingual compliance**: Both English and Chinese files submitted as required by the contribution guidelines.
- **Follows the template**: Covers all required sections (Integration Target, Prerequisites, Steps, Key Code, Caveats, References).
- **Index pages updated**: Both `docs/guide/integrations/index.md` and `docs/zh/guide/integrations/index.md` have the new entry appended.
- **Useful Before/After comparison**: The `exec()` → `Sandbox.run_code()` diff clearly communicates the value proposition.
- **Practical advanced scenarios**: Network isolation, persistent sandbox, and pause/resume sections add real depth.
- **Good caveats section**: Documents cold start latency, SDK scope limits, and network policy constraints honestly.

### Issues to address

1. **Unused `import json`** in the `create_cube_tool` snippet (`docs/guide/integrations/llamaindex.md:53` and the Chinese equivalent):
   ```python
   import json          # ← unused in this function
   from llama_index.core.tools import FunctionTool
   from cubesandbox import Sandbox, Config
   ```
   The `json` module is only used in the **"Going Further"** network policy snippet (a separate code block), not in `create_cube_tool` itself. Remove this import from the `create_cube_tool` block, or move it to the network policy snippet.

2. **`Sandbox.create(metadata=...)` without `config`** (`llamaindex.md:192-196` and ZH equivalent):
   ```python
   with Sandbox.create(
       metadata={"network-policy": "deny-all"}
   ) as sb:
   ```
   Earlier examples always pass `config=cfg` to `Sandbox.create()`. If the sandbox requires `Config` (template_id, api_url, etc.), this code would fail at runtime. Either:
   - Add a note that `Config` defaults are used, or
   - Include a `config=cfg` parameter alongside `metadata`.

3. **Optional: `template_id` example value** — The doc uses `python:3.12-slim` as the example template ID. If Cube Sandbox uses a different ID format than Docker image tags, this could mislead users. Worth verifying the actual template ID format.

4. **Optional: Redundant stop-word filter** in the WordFreq example (`llamaindex.md:157,161`):
   ```python
   self.skip = {'the','a','an','is','are','was','were','in','on','at','to','of','for'}
   # ...
   if w and w not in self.skip and len(w) > 3:
   ```
   Since `len(w) > 3` already excludes all 1-3 character words, most entries in `self.skip` (the, a, an, is, in, on, at, to, of, for) will never match. Only `are` and `was` (length 4) provide actual filtering. Consider either removing the `len(w) > 3` check or trimming the skip set to only 4+ letter stop words — whichever better reflects your intent.

---

Overall, this is a solid contribution. The content is accurate, well-organized, and follows project conventions. The issues above are minor and relate mostly to code quality in the examples.

@Johnny-zbb Thanks for submitting this LlamaIndex integration guide — the document structure is solid, and the bilingual (EN/ZH) coverage follows our contribution guidelines.

**I want to emphasize that integration tutorials must be verified against a real CubeSandbox deployment before submission**, otherwise incorrect examples can mislead other users and cause significant confusion. After reviewing the code examples in this PR, I found several issues that suggest they haven't been run against an actual CubeSandbox instance:

### Critical: Template ID format is incorrect

The document uses `template_id="python:3.12-slim"` in multiple places, but CubeSandbox template IDs are **auto-generated** in the format `tpl-<hex>` (e.g. `tpl-748094d2f2374b0a8a37e6ec`), not Docker image references. Users need to create a template via `cubemastercli tpl create-from-image` first, then copy the actual `template_id` from the command output. Passing `"python:3.12-slim"` would cause the API to return a 404 (TemplateNotFoundError).

See: [Creating Templates from OCI Images](https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/blob/master/docs/guide/tutorials/template-from-image.md) — Step 3 shows the correct usage: `export CUBE_TEMPLATE_ID=tpl-xxx`.

### Critical: Bare image lacks `envd` daemon

Even if someone tried to create a template from the `python:3.12-slim` image, it doesn't include `envd` — the CubeSandbox protocol endpoint — and would fail the readiness probe (`:49983/health` → 204). The correct approach is to:
- Build on top of `cubesandbox-base` (`FROM ghcr.io/tencentcloud/cubesandbox-base:2026.16`), or
- Inject `envd` and `cube-entrypoint.sh` via `COPY --from=cubesandbox-base` in your Dockerfile

See: [Bring Your Own Image (envd)](https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/blob/master/docs/guide/tutorials/bring-your-own-image.md)

### Other code issues

1. **`Sandbox.create(metadata=...)` missing `config`** — The network isolation examples in "Going Further" call `Sandbox.create(metadata={"network-policy": "deny-all"})` without passing `template` or `config`, which raises `ValueError` when env vars aren't set.
2. **Unused `import json`** — The `create_cube_tool` function imports `json` but never uses it (it's only used in a later network policy snippet).
3. **Prefer the SDK's native `network` parameter** — Use `Sandbox.create(network={"allow_out": [...], "deny_out": [...]})` instead of `metadata={"network-policy": ...}`. The `network` parameter is type-checked and more explicit.

### Suggestions

To ensure document quality, I'd recommend:
- Running the examples end-to-end against a real CubeSandbox deployment
- Replacing all instances of `"python:3.12-slim"` with either a real `tpl-*` template ID or the `<your-template-id>` placeholder, and noting that readers must create a template first
- Adding a template creation step to the Prerequisites section

Happy to help if you have questions about any of these points!

## Code Review: docs: add troubleshooting guide with 10 real-world entries

### Overview

This PR adds 10 bilingual (EN/ZH) troubleshooting articles to the Cube Sandbox documentation. Each article covers a real deployment or operations issue with a consistent **Symptom → Environment → Root Cause → Resolution → References** structure.

**1097 additions / 77 deletions across 22 files** — mostly new content, with two `index.md` files rewritten to include article tables.

### What's done well

- **Consistent structure**: Every article follows the `_template.md` format. Frontmatter, section headings, and content flow are uniform across all 10 articles.
- **Bilingual alignment**: Each English article has a matching Chinese counterpart with same filename, identical structure, and properly localized content. Chinese articles correctly use `/zh/` prefixed links.
- **Practical value**: All 10 articles describe real, reproducible issues with actionable resolution steps. Commands are copy-pasteable.
- **Index page redesign**: The empty "Published articles" placeholder table has been replaced with a filled table of the 10 new articles. The `_template.md` naming/frontmatter documentation was moved into the template itself, which is a cleaner approach.
- **VitePress compatibility**: The `srcExclude: ['**/_template.md']` config already handles template exclusion. The sidebar link to `/guide/troubleshooting/` resolves to `index.md` without additional config changes.

### Issues found

#### 1. `envd-stdout-truncated.md` — Python HTTP server blocks execution

**File**: `docs/guide/troubleshooting/envd-stdout-truncated.md:33-35`

```python
# Inside the sandbox, serve the file via HTTP
import subprocess
subprocess.run(["python3", "-m", "http.server", "8888"])
```

`subprocess.run()` is a blocking call. If this is submitted via envd `exec`, it will hang waiting for the server to exit. If it's meant to be run inside the sandbox shell interactively, the snippet is fine as-is, but this context isn't clear.

**Suggestion**: Either add `&` to the bash equivalent, or mention that the HTTP server should be started in a separate terminal/session.

#### 2. `pvm-enable-overridden-by-env.md` — Missing edge case for absent `.env`

**File**: `docs/guide/troubleshooting/pvm-enable-overridden-by-env.md:27-28`

The root cause covers the case where `.env` exists with `CUBE_PVM_ENABLE=0`, but doesn't mention what happens if `.env` doesn't exist at all. Does the installer create it? Will the env var be respected?

**Suggestion**: Add a note clarifying that if `.env` doesn't exist, the environment variable is used directly (or state the installer's behavior explicitly).

#### 3. `pvm-enable-overridden-by-env.md` — Bilingual references section mismatch

**English** (lines 50-52): References split across two lines
```markdown
- Related docs: [PVM Deployment](/guide/pvm-deploy)
- Related issue: [#147](https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/issues/147)
```

**Chinese**: Combined on one line
```markdown
- 相关文档: [PVM部署](/zh/guide/pvm-deploy), 相关 issue: [#147](https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/issues/147)
```

Minor inconsistency — the Chinese version combines two reference items on one line while the English version uses separate lines.

#### 4. `insufficient-disk-space.md` — Destructive Docker prune without warning

**File**: `docs/guide/troubleshooting/insufficient-disk-space.md:39`

```bash
docker system prune -f
docker volume prune -f
```

`docker system prune -f` removes all unused containers, networks, images, and build cache. Adding `docker volume prune -f` also removes all unused volumes, which can delete persistent data that might be needed later.

**Suggestion**: Add a brief warning note that `docker volume prune -f` will remove all unused volumes and their data. Suggest using `docker system prune -f` alone as a safer first step.

#### 5. `kvm-pvm-missing-after-reboot.md` — `lsmod` expected output removed in Chinese version

**English** (lines 36-38): Shows expected `lsmod` output
```bash
lsmod | grep kvm_pvm
# Expected output:
# kvm_pvm                49152  10
# kvm                   1175552  1 kvm_pvm
```

**Chinese** (lines 34-35): No expected output shown
```bash
lsmod | grep kvm_pvm
```

**Suggestion**: Add the expected output to the Chinese version for consistency.

#### 6. `envd-stdout-truncated.md` — Vague reference

**File**: `docs/guide/troubleshooting/envd-stdout-truncated.md:43`

```
- Related issue: Host mount and file transfer discussions
```

This is not a specific, actionable reference. If there's a GitHub issue number, use it. Otherwise, this should link to a relevant docs page.

### Minor suggestions

- **Tags capitalization**: Some tags use lowercase (`deployment`, `template`) while others use uppercase (`PVM`, `DNS`) or mixed (`Basic Auth`). Consider standardizing tag casing for consistency.
- **zh index.md title change**: The Chinese index title changed from "故障**排障**" to "故障**排查**". Both are valid, but "故障排障" is somewhat redundant (障 appears twice). The new title "故障排查" reads better.

### Summary

This is a solid documentation PR. The content is practical, well-structured, and properly bilingual. The issues above are minor — mostly consistency nits and one functional concern about the Python snippet. With those addressed, this is ready to merge.

+---
+title: 重启后 kvm_pvm 模块未加载
+author: yeezon

+
+# 重启后 kvm_pvm 模块未加载
+
+## 症状
+
+模板构建在最后阶段报 `expected:VsockServerReady, actual:VmShutdown`，VM 启动后立即关闭。服务器重启后出现，此前 PVM 工作正常。
+
+## 环境
+
+- Cube Sandbox 版本: v0.2.0
+- 相关组件:  PVM,  Ubuntu 24.04 LTS / OpenCloudOS 9
+
+## 根因
+
+`kvm_pvm` 内核模块只是手动加载了，未配置开机自启。服务器重启后模块丢失，PVM 能力不可用。没有 `kvm_pvm`，Hypervisor 无法创建 MicroVM，Guest 内核立即崩溃。
+
+## 解决方法
+
+```bash
+# 立即加载模块
+modprobe kvm_pvm
+
+# 验证已加载
+lsmod | grep kvm_pvm
+
+# 配置开机自动加载
+echo 'kvm_pvm' > /etc/modules-load.d/kvm-pvm.conf
+```
+
+加载模块后，重启受影响的服务：
+
+```bash
+cd /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/one-click/
+bash down.sh && sleep 2 && bash up.sh
+```

comments.body:
Thank you for your very detailed proposal. I think we can only support EROFS for container images, as the usage of guest images is extremely limited in our design. In typical scenarios, there should only be one guest image globally, which should be pre-deployed on each computing node and shared with all sandboxes through pmem. EROFS almost does not bring any benefits to the guest image, so we can focus on the container image scenario. In fact, we do use EROFS to support container images internally.

 @charliecgxu @ls-ggg @hlz260 @zhuangel Do you have any suggestions?

I agree with you. Since multiple sandboxes share a single Guest OS rootfs, the gains are pretty minimal, and we'd lose the DAX capability. Let's keep our proposal focused on the container rootfs instead.

I've updated the version, PTAL @kinwin-ustc

This is a valuable and practical design proposal, and I really appreciate your efforts in exploring EROFS integration to further improve storage efficiency and cold startup performance for CubeSandbox.
Meanwhile I have a few points for further discussion:
Firstly, it would be nice to clarify whether we keep the traditional layered OCI image structure or adopt a flattened EROFS layout for workload rootfs. This decision will have impacts on our existing image building and distribution pipelines.
Secondly, if EROFS is utilized together with virtio-blk inside guest, we may face some constraints in resource sharing. In this way, it is hard to realize unified disk space sharing and host-side page cache sharing across different sandbox instances. The page cache will be isolated inside each guest system, which may bring extra storage and memory cost in large-scale scenarios, and cannot well take advantage of the shared cache capability of the current virtio-fs architecture.
Looking forward to your further ideas on these aspects.

Thanks for your reply! These are indeed two critical issues (here are my current thoughts based on my understanding, and please feel free to correct me if I missed anything).

In this initial proposal, I kept it relatively simple: positioning EROFS as a **complementary option to ext4+DAX**, specifically tailored for scenarios where reducing disk footprint and network transfer size is the top priority. We have no intention of replacing ext4+DAX entirely. For memory-sensitive workloads that heavily rely on shared cache, ext4+DAX remains the go-to choice for performance.

**Layered OCI vs. Flattened EROFS Layout**
The containerd community's [EROFS Snapshotter](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/main/docs/snapshotters/erofs.md) typically builds a `layer.erofs` for each OCI layer, adopting such a multi-device mounting scheme poses clear limitations under CubeSandbox's current MicroVM rootfs injection path:
* **Hypervisor Device Slot Limits:** Stacking multiple device layers requires dynamically hot-plugging a virtual block device (like vPMEM or virtio-blk) for each layer. Standard OCI images easily have 10-20+ layers, which would quickly exhaust the limited PCI/device slots in Cloud-Hypervisor (clh) and even lead to MicroVM boot failures.
* **Cold Start Overhead:** Forcing the Guest kernel to mount dozens of devices and stack them via OverlayFS introduces significant boot latency, which defeats the purpose of MicroVMs' ultra-fast cold starts.
* **Upstream MicroVM Image Format Limits:** While runc containers can easily leverage flattened filesystems, passing layered structures into MicroVMs usually requires an extra flattening mechanism or formats like [VMDK](https://github.com/containerd/nerdbox/issues/30). However, the proposal to support VMDK in Cloud-Hypervisor ([#7167](https://github.com/cloud-hypervisor/cloud-hypervisor/issues/7167)) is currently stalled.

**Page Cache Sharing & Resource Constraints (Compression vs. DAX)**
The Page Cache isolation issue is indeed present. I understand this as a fundamental technical trade-off: **ext4+DAX bypasses the Guest Page Cache to minimize duplicate cache overhead**, whereas **compressed EROFS focuses on extreme storage and bandwidth savings**.
Because compressed data must be decompressed within the Guest's memory, we cannot directly leverage the DAX path like ext4+DAX does. As a result, Page Cache is isolated within each Guest instance, which indeed increases memory cost under high-density deployments compared to virtio-fs or ext4+DAX.

**Future Evolution**
Internally, we are also actively exploring rootfs solutions for MicroVM scenarios. We've been particularly inspired by the work Nydus has done around native lazy-pulling (e.g., [EROFS over Fscache On-demand Loading Technology](https://www.alibabacloud.com/blog/faster-container-image-loading-speed-with-nydus-rafs-and-erofs_599012)) and are currently validating several related approaches.

One promising direction we see is an architecture combining EROFS, Nydus, and ublk/io_uring-based userspace block backends, enabling both efficient lazy pulling and high-density MicroVM deployments while minimizing userspace overhead and context-switch costs.

I heard that your team has also been utilizing EROFS for container rootfs in your environments. Could you share some of your experiences?

EROFS supports erofs+fsdax too, but as mentioned, compressed data cannot be used as DAX because compressed data cannot be directly used for mmap.
I think one solution is that we could convert EROFS compressed data on-the-fly on the host (the metadata is also generated/converted on demand) and provide a converted uncompressed filesystem so that it can be shared with guests instead.

EROFS over fscache is now deprecated, the future direction is to leverage fanotify pre-content hooks + eBPF to work out a similar approach.

If it is only a matter of replacing ext4 with erofs, using the compression mechanism of erofs to reduce disk storage and distribution bandwidth, and using the computing and memory resources inside the sandbox to exchange for storage resources on the host, this solution does not have universal value. First, the existing ext4 can perform layer-level deduplication at the host level, while as you described, if erofs uses the layer scheme, there will be issues with the number of devices, and using the flat scheme will lose the deduplication capability; second, if only the distribution bandwidth is considered, compressed distribution can be considered, and then decompressed locally into ext4, and now the network bandwidth of data centers is very large, basically already over 100Gbps, I believe that physical limitations will not be a big problem in terms of throughput. 

As for the greater value of EROFS, I believe it lies in utilizing the natural chunk mechanism of EROFS to perform chunk-level deduplication and lazy loading, which will bring significant benefits in terms of actual storage consumption, bandwidth consumption, and cold start speed.

> the existing ext4 can perform layer-level deduplication at the host level

how? you mean ext4 unpacking + overlayfs or some other alternatives? how does this approach pass into the guest, virtiofs? that performance will be bad. -- I don't get the overall point.

> if erofs uses the layer scheme, there will be issues with the number of devices, and using the flat scheme will lose the deduplication capability

I don't know if these words relate to CubeSandbox or just runC.
First, since Linux v6.12, erofs supports file-backed mounts, so if it's a runc usage, you could just mount the layer file directly without loopback block devices.

As for microVMs, currently many people are working on fsmerge/GPT + vmdk feature for virtio-blk/virtio-pmem, like:
https://github.com/containerd/nerdbox/issues/30
https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/pull/12763
https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/pull/12958
https://github.com/firecracker-microvm/firecracker/pull/5741
there won't be per-layer block/pmem devices in the guest for layer deduplication; only one block device with merged view for each instance is needed. (regarding to fsmerge, see: https://erofs.docs.kernel.org/en/latest/merging.html)

If FSDAX+erofs is enabled, the page cache will be shared in the per-layer basis (rather than per-image basis).

> and now the network bandwidth of data centers is very large, basically already over 100Gbps, I believe that physical limitations will not be a big problem in terms of throughput.

It only works within a private network, and object-storage-based OCI registries won't reach such limitation at all.
Also some users need to distribute/publish their images over the public network too, so network traffic saving + public network quality is important for some users.

>> the existing ext4 can perform layer-level deduplication at the host level
> how? you mean ext4 unpacking + overlayfs or some other alternatives? how does this approach pass into the guest, virtiofs? that performance will be bad. -- I don't get the overall point.

## Description
This PR introduces a comprehensive design proposal for integrating **EROFS (Enhanced Read-Only File System)** into the CubeSandbox runtime for **container Rootfs artifacts**. The goal is to optimize storage efficiency, distribution speed, and cold-start performance for read-only layers.

### Key Highlights:
- **End-to-End Lifecycle**: Defines the integration from CubeMaster build pipeline to Cubelet distribution and CubeShim runtime mount execution.
- **Engineering Hardening**: Specifies mandatory `erofs-utils` versioning (>= 1.5.0) and xattr support to preserve OverlayFS metadata (Whiteouts).
- **Performance & Observability**: Outlines a detailed benchmarking plan and critical metrics (compression ratios, cold-start latency) for production readiness.

**Note**: In this proposal, the Guest OS rootfs remains using the existing **ext4** scheme to maintain stability, while workload Rootfs artifacts are extended to support EROFS.

## Related Issues
Relates to #274

## Code Review: Fix ext4 artifact runtime file materialization for PVM templates

This is a well-structured fix for a clear production bug. The core change — replacing a strict validation (`validateArtifactRuntimeFilesPresent`) with a proactive materialization step (`ensureArtifactRuntimeFiles`) — is the right approach. The tests are thorough and the e2e validation in the PR description is convincing.

### Positive aspects

- **Clear architectural separation**: `ensureArtifactRuntimeFiles` tries validation first, falls back to materialization, then re-validates. This handles both the "fresh artifact with no runtime files" case and the "existing artifact with valid runtime files" case.
- **Atomic file operations**: Both `copyLocalFileAtomically` (utils.go:197) and `copyKernelFileAtomically` (kernel_sync.go:164) use the write-to-`.`tmp`-then-`os.Rename` pattern, which is correct for crash safety on Linux (same-filesystem `Rename` is atomic).
- **Exhaustive test coverage**: Nine test cases covering materialization, preservation of existing files, standalone rootfs validation, and error paths for missing shared sources.

### Suggestions (minor)

**1. Redundant final validation in `ensureArtifactRuntimeFiles`** (utils.go:138-152)

After refreshing the kernel and version files, the function calls `validateArtifactRuntimeFilesPresent` which re-validates both files. This is a safe defense-in-depth pattern, but you could remove the final validation call to save two `stat` calls and a `sameFileSHA256` check on the happy path:

```
EnsurePmemRootfs
→ ensureKernelFilePresent (stats kernel → missing)
→ refreshKernelFile (copies + SHA256 validates)
→ validateImageVersionFilePresent (stats version → missing)
→ refreshImageVersionFile (copies + validates non-empty)
// validateArtifactRuntimeFilesPresent is implicit since
// the two refresh functions already verify correctness
```

This is not a correctness issue — just a minor observation about double-validation on the critical path. The existing code is safer if either refresh function has a subtle bug.

**2. Code duplication in atomic copy** (utils.go:197 vs kernel_sync.go:164)

`copyLocalFileAtomically` in utils.go is structurally identical to `copyKernelFileAtomically` in kernel_sync.go. The difference is only the log message. Since `copyLocalFileAtomically` is `unexported` and within the same module, you could have reused the `pmem` package version if it were exported. Not worth blocking the PR, but worth noting for a follow-up cleanup.

**3. Minor test gap** (utils_test.go:129-148)

`TestEnsurePmemFileMaterializesMissingKernelFile` does not set up a version file and does not assert that one was materialized. Because `ensureArtifactRuntimeFiles` processes kernel first then version, and the shared version file IS written (line 135), the version file *will* be materialized — but the test doesn't verify it. Consider adding a version assertion to this test (or a combined test that verifies both are materialized when neither exists).

### No security concerns

- Path traversal risks are addressed by `pathutil.ValidateSafeID` (utils.go:41-44) and the `// NOCC:Path Traversal()` annotations on file operations.
- No user-controlled data is written to disk without validation.
- No unsafe defer-in-loop patterns or leaked file descriptors.

### Summary

The fix is correct, well-tested, and addresses the reported bug. Ship it with or without the minor suggestions above.

## Summary

- materialize missing ext4 artifact runtime companion files in `EnsurePmemFile`
- refresh the artifact-local kernel from the shared kernel when `<artifact>.vm` is absent
- refresh the artifact-local image `version` from the shared image version when absent
- update regression tests for missing `.vm` and `version` materialization

## Problem

On a clean v0.2.1 one-click PVM deployment, template creation can fail during the distribution phase after the ext4 rootfs artifact has been built. Cubelet validates that the artifact-local kernel file already exists, but the artifact directory may only contain the generated `.ext4` file.

Observed failure:

```text
[5/7] DISTRIBUTING progress=100% distribution=0/1 ready, 1 failed
artifact distribution failed on all 1 nodes: cubelet create image on 192.168.0.153 failed:
pull image rfs-85b1d8fade9ebd6a5c8fc9b7: ensure pmem file failed:
target kernel file /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/rfs-85b1d8fade9ebd6a5c8fc9b7/rfs-85b1d8fade9ebd6a5c8fc9b7.vm not exist
```

Before the fix, the artifact directory contained only:

```text
rfs-85b1d8fade9ebd6a5c8fc9b7.ext4
```

## Fix

`EnsurePmemFile` now keeps the existing rootfs check, then ensures the runtime companion files are present. If the artifact-local kernel or image version is missing or invalid, Cubelet refreshes them from the shared runtime files and then performs the existing final validation. Existing artifact-local runtime files are preserved.

## Verification

Unit/static verification:

```text
git diff --check
GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go test -c ./internal/cube/server/images/ext4image ./pkg/container/pmem
```

Linux container tests:

```text
go test ./internal/cube/server/images/ext4image ./pkg/container/pmem
ok github.com/tencentcloud/CubeSandbox/Cubelet/internal/cube/server/images/ext4image
ok github.com/tencentcloud/CubeSandbox/Cubelet/pkg/container/pmem
```

End-to-end clean PVM validation on a fresh VM:

- OS: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS
- Host kernel after PVM setup: `6.6.69-cube.pvm.host.005.x-gb85200d80fa2`
- `kvm_pvm` loaded and `/dev/kvm` present
- Installed official v0.2.1 one-click deployment with `CUBE_PVM_ENABLE=1`
- Reproduced the original `.vm not exist` failure with the unmodified Cubelet
- Replaced only the Cubelet binary with this patch
- Re-ran template creation for the same image/artifact path

Patched result:

```text
[6/7] CREATING_TEMPLATE progress=85% distribution=1/1 ready, 0 failed
[7/7] READY progress=100% distribution=1/1 ready, 0 failed
template image job succeeded
```

The patched Cubelet materialized both files:

```text
rfs-85b1d8fade9ebd6a5c8fc9b7.ext4
rfs-85b1d8fade9ebd6a5c8fc9b7.vm
version
```

The generated `.vm` SHA256 matched the shared kernel, and the generated artifact `version` matched the shared image version.

comments.body:
Hi @vwxyzjn, thanks a lot for this PR — the implementation is quite complete, covering CLI / API / CubeMaster / Cubelet / cgroup v1 & v2 in one go, and the unit tests are nicely done. While reviewing it I have a few questions I'd like to align on, mainly to make sure we understand the actual benefit this feature delivers in cubebox's current form.

### 1. How host-level burst takes effect under the cubebox form factor

Looking at the current implementation, `cpu.max.burst` / `cpu.cfs_burst_us` is written to the **host cgroup that wraps the VMM process**. However, cubebox today only has a single instance form, `InstanceType_cubebox` — essentially a VM whose vCPU count is fixed at template/snapshot time and is aligned with `resources.cpu` (see `GetResourceWithOverhead` in `Cubelet/plugins/cube/internals/cgroup/cgroup.go`).

This makes me unsure about the observable effect of burst on the guest side. For example, with `cpu=2` and `host_burst.cpu=4`, only 2 vCPU threads inside the VM can actually do work; when the cubebox cgroup is fully loaded on the host, total usage is roughly `2 + a bit for VMM helper threads`, which is still quite far from 4. So I'd like to confirm:

- Which scenario do you primarily expect this burst to serve? Smoothing out spikes from VMM / IO helper threads, or a measurable throughput / latency improvement for the workload inside the guest?
- If the goal is the latter, wouldn't burst be more effective if it were applied to the **inner cgroup inside the guest**? My concern is that host-level burst under a VM form factor may not produce a measurable difference on the guest side.

If you have a different understanding or any references on this, happy to align.

### 2. Validation data

The Validation section in the PR description consists entirely of `go test` / `go test -c`, which I think is enough for correctness. Before merging, could you provide a set of real-machine e2e numbers? Something along these lines would be sufficient:

- Run on a Linux box whose kernel supports `cpu.cfs_burst_us` / `cpu.max.burst`;
- Run a CPU-saturating workload (sysbench cpu, fio, or a concrete business cold-start case), once with `host_burst.cpu = cpu` and once with `host_burst.cpu = 2*cpu`;
- Share `nr_bursts` / `burst_time` from the host-side `cpu.stat` (to confirm bursts actually occurred), plus guest-side CPU usage and benchmark results.

This will help us evaluate the real value of the feature for users.

### 3. A small naming suggestion

The `host_burst.cpu` field exposes the "host" layer to API users, but users typically only think in terms of containers and aren't aware of the host / VM split. If we decide to keep this feature, would it make sense to rename the field to something more neutral (e.g. `resources.burst.cpu`) and clearly document the layer it applies to (host cgroup vs. guest cgroup)? This is a nit — we can address it after the overall direction is settled.

Overall I'd like to align on points 1 and 2 first. Looking forward to your reply, thanks!

item.body:
## Summary

Adds an optional per-container `resources.host_burst.cpu` field. CubeMaster aggregates the per-container burst ceilings into `cube.master.instance.host_cpu_burst` and leaves `resources.cpu` as the normal scheduler/request CPU.

Cubelet stores the normal host quota in `HostCpuQ`, stores the burst ceiling in `HostCpuBurstQ`, and converts the difference into the cgroup burst file:

- cgroup v2: `cpu.max.burst`
- cgroup v1, when supported by the kernel: `cpu.cfs_burst_us`

The API validates `host_burst.cpu >= cpu` and `host_burst.cpu <= 2 * cpu`, matching cgroup burst credit limits. For example, `cpu=2` and `host_burst.cpu=4` keeps average CPU at 2 while allowing bounded burst credit up to 4 CPUs.

Also adds `cubemastercli tpl create-from-image --host-burst-cpu` so template authors can set the burst ceiling when creating templates from images.

## Validation

- `go test ./pkg/service/sandbox -run 'TestCheckAndGetContainers'`
- `go test ./pkg/service/httpservice/cube -run '^$'`
- `GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go test -c -o /tmp/cubelet-cgroup.test ./plugins/cube/internals/cgroup`
- `GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go test -c -o /tmp/cubelet-cgroup-handle-v1.test ./plugins/cube/internals/cgroup/handle/v1`
- `GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go test -c -o /tmp/cubelet-cgroup-handle-v2.test ./plugins/cube/internals/cgroup/handle/v2`
- `GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go test -c -o /tmp/cubelet-services-cubebox.test ./services/cubebox`
- `GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go test -c -o /tmp/cubelet-store-cubebox.test ./pkg/store/cubebox`
- `GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go test -c -o /tmp/cubemastercli-cubebox.test ./cmd/cubemastercli/commands/cubebox`
- `git diff --check`

Note: `go test ./cmd/cubemastercli/commands/cubebox -run 'TestParseContainerOverrides'` does not compile on this Darwin/arm64 host because the package depends on `github.com/agiledragon/gomonkey`, which fails with `undefined: buildJmpDirective` for this local toolchain. The Linux compile check above passes.
